q: When is the Island ferry busiest?

queries.purpose: Average riders per day by month (complete years 2016-2025)
queries.sql: SELECT strftime(d, '%b') AS label, round(avg(day_total)) AS value FROM (SELECT date_trunc('day', ts) AS d, sum(tickets_redeemed) AS day_total FROM ferry WHERE year(ts) BETWEEN 2016 AND 2025 GROUP BY 1) GROUP BY month(d), strftime(d, '%b') ORDER BY month(d)

queries.purpose: Average riders per day by day of week (summer, Jun-Aug, 2016-2025)
queries.sql: SELECT strftime(d, '%a') AS label, round(avg(day_total)) AS value FROM (SELECT date_trunc('day', ts) AS d, sum(tickets_redeemed) AS day_total FROM ferry WHERE year(ts) BETWEEN 2016 AND 2025 AND month(ts) IN (6,7,8) GROUP BY 1) GROUP BY isodow(d), strftime(d, '%a') ORDER BY isodow(d)

queries.purpose: Average riders per hour of day (summer, Jun-Aug, 2016-2025)
queries.sql: SELECT lpad(CAST(h AS VARCHAR), 2, '0') || ':00' AS label, round(sum(tickets_redeemed) * 1.0 / count(DISTINCT d)) AS value FROM (SELECT hour(ts) AS h, date_trunc('day', ts) AS d, tickets_redeemed FROM ferry WHERE year(ts) BETWEEN 2016 AND 2025 AND month(ts) IN (6,7,8)) GROUP BY h ORDER BY h

story.lead: Summer Saturdays around noon are the busiest.
story.summary: The ferry is busiest in August, with about **9,768** riders a day. Saturdays in summer are the peak, at about **12,513** riders, and the midday hours from 11:00 to 13:00 are the busiest. August is about **20 times** busier than January (**492** a day).
story.sub: Island ferry tickets used, 2016 to 2025 (complete years), counted in 15-minute intervals.

facts.label: average riders a day in August
average riders on a summer Saturday
riders in the noon hour on a summer day

points.h: August is the peak, July close behind
points.p: Daily riders climb from **492** in January to **9,768** in August. July is also very busy at **8,699** a day. By October it drops to **2,043**.

points.h: Weekends are about double a summer weekday
points.p: On summer Saturdays the ferry carries **12,513** riders a day, and on Sundays **11,518**. Tuesday is the quietest at **5,521**. Friday, at **7,257**, is the busiest weekday.

points.h: Riders build up through the morning, peak at noon
points.p: On an average summer day about **995** people board in the noon hour. The 11:00 hour is almost as busy at **986**. After 15:00 it fades, with **247** at 19:00 and almost nobody overnight.

story.note: These are averages over ten years of tickets used, so single days can be much busier or quieter.

q: Which subway stations have the most delays?

queries.purpose: Stations with the most delays (incidents with delay minutes above 0)
queries.sql: SELECT station AS label, count(*) AS value FROM subway_delays WHERE min_delay > 0 AND station IS NOT NULL GROUP BY station ORDER BY value DESC LIMIT 15

queries.purpose: Stations with the most total delay minutes
queries.sql: SELECT station AS label, sum(min_delay) AS value FROM subway_delays WHERE min_delay > 0 AND station IS NOT NULL GROUP BY station ORDER BY value DESC LIMIT 15

queries.purpose: Stations with the longest average delay (stations with at least 30 delays)
queries.sql: SELECT station AS label, round(avg(min_delay), 1) AS value FROM subway_delays WHERE min_delay > 0 AND station IS NOT NULL GROUP BY station HAVING count(*) >= 30 ORDER BY value DESC LIMIT 15

story.lead: Kipling station had the most subway delays.
story.summary: Kipling had **578** delays, just ahead of Kennedy (**537**) and Wilson (**513**). But Eglinton lost the most time overall, **4,001** minutes, which is about 67 hours. The "worst" station depends on whether you count how often or how long.
story.sub: TTC subway delay incidents with at least one minute of delay, 1 January 2025 to 31 August 2026.

facts.label: delays at Kipling, the most of any station
total delay at Eglinton, the most of any station
average delay at Woodbine, the longest

points.h: Kipling, Kennedy and Wilson top the list for delays
points.p: Kipling had **578** delays, Kennedy **537** and Wilson **513**. Bloor (**504**) and Finch (**464**) are close behind. After the top six, the counts drop to **336** or fewer.

points.h: Eglinton lost the most minutes in total
points.p: Eglinton added up to **4,001** minutes of delay, ahead of Kipling at **3,461**. Victoria Park and Sheppard West each passed **3,000** minutes without being among the top five for number of delays.

points.h: Woodbine delays last longest on average
points.p: Delays at Woodbine averaged **12.3** minutes, with Sheppard West at **12** and Islington at **11.9**. Eglinton averaged **9** minutes, so its high total comes from both many delays and long ones. Only stations with at least 30 delays are included.

story.note: Only incidents with more than zero minutes of delay are counted, and there are no passenger numbers, so busier stations are not adjusted for.

story.lead: Luna is Toronto's top dog name now, ahead of Charlie.
story.summary: In 2025, **549** licensed dogs were named Luna, more than any other name. Charlie came second with **491**, but Charlie was the top name on average across 2020 to 2025 (**529** a year). Charlie's yearly count has slipped from a peak of **595** in 2021.

facts.label: licensed dogs named Luna in 2025
Charlie's yearly average, 2020–2025, the highest
Charlie's count, 2021 to 2025

points.h: Luna led in 2025, with Charlie second
points.p: **549** dogs were named Luna and **491** were named Charlie. Bella was third with **386**. Luna had about two and a half times as many dogs as 15th-place Lola (**217**).

points.h: Over six years, Charlie edges out Luna
points.p: Averaged over 2020 to 2025, Charlie comes first with **529** dogs a year, and Luna second with **493**. Bella is third with **405**. Luna's 2025 count (**549**) is above its six-year average.

points.h: Charlie peaked in 2021 and has since dropped
points.p: Charlie hit **595** dogs in 2021. By 2025 it was **491**, about 17% lower. The count has held roughly steady since 2023.

story.note: These counts cover licensed dogs only, and only the 200 most common names each year.

story.lead: Electrical failure is the top known fire cause
story.summary: The most common answer on record is "undetermined", with **4,012** fires. Among fires with a known cause, electrical failure is first with **3,134** fires, ahead of improperly discarded items (**2,255**). Fires left unattended hurt the most people: **350** civilian casualties, about double the next cause.
story.sub: Toronto Fire Services fires (not outdoor no-loss fires), 2011 to 2024.

facts.label: fires caused by electrical failure, top known cause
fires with an undetermined cause
civilian casualties from unattended fires

points.h: Undetermined is the most common recorded cause
points.p: Fire crews could not pin down a cause for **4,012** fires, more than any named cause. Electrical failure is next with **3,134**, then improperly discarded items with **2,255**.

points.h: Electrical failure leads once unknowns are removed
points.p: Without the undetermined fires, electrical failure is first with **3,134** fires. That is about **1.4 times** as many as improperly discarded items (**2,255**). Several labels sound alike, such as "other unintended cause" and "other unintentional cause, not classified", and are counted separately.

points.h: Unattended fires caused the most casualties
points.p: Fires left unattended led to **350** civilian casualties, about **twice** the next cause, improper handling of ignition sources (**170**). Electrical failure follows closely with **164**.

story.note: Causes are counted under the labels as recorded, and some labels overlap, so each bar is a count for that label only. Casualties means civilians hurt or killed, as recorded.

story.lead: King is the most-delayed streetcar route.
story.summary: The 504 King streetcar had more delays than any other route: **3,269** between January 2025 and August 2026. The 501 Queen was almost level with it, at **3,255**. Dundas and Carlton follow, well behind. Next we look at how often routes were held up, how much time was lost, and how long each hold-up lasted.
story.sub: TTC streetcar delays with at least one minute lost, 1 January 2025 to 31 August 2026.

facts.label: delays on the 504 King, the most
minutes lost on the 504 King
average minutes per delay on 301 Queen Night

points.h: King and Queen are almost tied at the top
points.p: Counting delays gives a very close race. The 504 King had **3,269** and the 501 Queen had **3,255**, only 14 apart. Dundas (**2,491**) and Carlton (**2,349**) came next. Kingston Road was fifth with **1,552**, so the top four stand well clear of the rest.

points.h: King takes the lead once lost time is added up
points.p: Counting minutes, King pulls ahead. Its delays added up to **77,703** minutes, against **74,034** for Queen. That is about 3,700 minutes more. Dundas (**59,316**) and Carlton (**56,379**) stay third and fourth. The order at the top matches the order by number of delays, so King is the most-delayed route on both counts.

points.h: Night routes have the longest single delays
points.p: The delays on a route can be short or long. The night routes were the worst: the 301 Queen Night lost **35** minutes per delay on average, and the 306 Carlton Night lost **31.8**. Among the busy daytime routes, Carlton (**24**), Dundas and King (**23.8** each) lost the most time per delay. Spadina had the shortest, at **14.9** minutes. So King is hit often, and each delay costs a good deal of time.

story.takeaway: The 504 King comes out on top for both the number of delays and the minutes lost, with Queen close behind. Dundas and Carlton follow. Night routes have the longest delays each time, but they have far fewer of them.
story.note: Only incidents with at least one minute of delay are counted, and the data does not say how many riders were affected.

story.lead: Shelter use peaked in 2024 and has fallen since.
story.summary: In 2024, an average of **9,766** people stayed in Toronto shelters each night, the highest year in this data. By September 2026 the nightly number was **7,324**, about a quarter lower than that peak. Still, that is more people than the **6,382** a night in 2021.
story.sub: Nightly shelter counts, City of Toronto, 1 Jan 2021 to 4 Oct 2026 (2026 is a partial year).

facts.label: people a night in 2024, the highest year
people a night in September 2026
people a night in mixed adult shelters, 2025

points.h: Nightly numbers rose until 2024, then dropped
points.p: The average went from **6,382** people a night in 2021 to **9,766** in 2024. It then fell to **9,215** in 2025 and **8,209** so far in 2026.

points.h: Winters are busier, and 2026 has fallen month after month
points.p: Each winter is higher than the summer around it. January 2025 hit **10,228** people a night, while January 2026 was **9,217**. Since February 2026 it has fallen every month, to **7,324** in September 2026.

points.h: Mixed adult and family shelters hold the most people
points.p: In 2025, mixed adult shelters averaged **2,831** people a night and family shelters **2,484**. Men's shelters had **2,099**, women's **1,082** and youth **719**.

story.note: Each number is the average of the nightly totals across all shelter programs, counting people, not beds.

story.lead: Gibraltar Point Beach was the safest for swimming.
story.summary: Gibraltar Point Beach had the fewest unsafe days since 2021: only **4.3%** of days were over the City's limit of 100 E. coli. Sunnyside Beach was unsafe on **36.8%** of days, about eight and a half times as often.
story.sub: Toronto beach water tests, swimming seasons (May to September) from 2021 to 2026.

facts.label: Days unsafe at Gibraltar Point, the lowest
Days unsafe at Sunnyside, the highest
Share the lowest typical level, 14 E. coli

points.h: Gibraltar Point, Hanlan's Point and Cherry Beach were unsafe least often
points.p: Gibraltar Point was unsafe on **4.3%** of days, then Hanlan's Point at **6.6%** and Cherry Beach at **7.7%**. At the other end, Centre Island, Marie Curtis Park East and Sunnyside were each unsafe on more than a third of days.

points.h: Four beaches share the lowest typical bacteria level
points.p: Gibraltar Point, Ward's Island, Hanlan's Point and Cherry Beach all have a typical level of **14**. Sunnyside's typical level is **74**, about five times higher, but still under the limit of 100.

points.h: Every beach has about 600 or more days of tests
points.p: Counts run from **601** days at Gibraltar Point to **651** at Woodbine Beaches. Each beach has a similar, large amount of testing behind it, so the comparison is fair.

story.note: A day counts as unsafe when the average E. coli across a beach's test sites is above 100 per 100 mL; results can change from day to day.

story.lead: Pothole complaints in 2026 are the highest on record
story.summary: Toronto got **23,976** pothole requests in just the first eight months of 2026. That is already more than any full year since 2019, and about **two and a half times** the same months of 2025. Numbers swing a lot from year to year.
story.sub: 311 pothole requests, 2019 to August 2026 (2026 covers January to August only).

facts.label: pothole requests, Jan–Aug 2026
requests in 2021, the lowest year
requests in March 2026, the busiest month in the last two years

points.h: 2026 has already passed every earlier full year
points.p: Yearly requests rose and fell: **18,495** in 2019, down to **4,432** in 2021, then up to **15,578** in 2023. 2026 has only eight months counted and is already at **23,976**, above all of them.

points.h: Complaints peak in late winter, then fade
points.p: In an average year, March is the busiest month with about **2,706** requests. By November it drops to about **359**, roughly **one-seventh** as many. February to April carry the most complaints.

points.h: Early 2026 was far busier than early 2025
points.p: February 2026 had **5,067** requests, about **four times** the **1,244** in February 2025. March 2026 reached **6,227**, nearly double March 2025 (**3,250**). By August the gap had narrowed: **629** against **563**.

story.note: Requests are counted under both the old and new City names for potholes. 2026 is only January to August, so the full year will end higher.

story.lead: About 40 cyclists a year are seriously hurt or killed
story.summary: Over the last ten full years, an average of about **39** cyclists a year were killed or seriously injured in Toronto crashes. The yearly count has fallen from a peak of **68** in 2012 to **33** in 2025. Most of the harm happens in warm months, when cycling is busiest.
story.sub: Toronto police collision data (killed or seriously injured), people on bikes, 2006–2025 full years.

facts.label: cyclists killed or seriously hurt per year, 2016–2025
the 2012 peak, versus 33 in 2025
cyclists killed in 2024, the most in any year

points.h: Serious cyclist injuries are lower than ten years ago
points.p: The number of cyclists killed or seriously injured peaked at **68** in 2012. It dropped to a low of **21** in 2021. In 2025 it was **33**, about half the 2012 level, though it went up and down along the way.

points.h: Deaths are few each year, but 2024 stood out
points.p: Most years, between one and four cyclists were killed. In 2024 the number reached **7**, the highest in the 20 years shown. In 2025 it fell back to **2**.

points.h: Summer is by far the most dangerous season
points.p: June has the most, at **5.5** people a year on average, against **0.8** in January. May to September together make up about **64%** of the year's total.

story.note: Only cyclists who were killed or had major injuries are counted, and each person counts once. 2026 is left out because the year is not complete.

story.lead: Closures are rare: about one inspection in 1,000
story.summary: Of about 80,500 restaurant and food-shop inspections, only **82** ended with the place being closed. That is about **0.1%**, or roughly one in a thousand. Most inspections end in a clean pass (**75,678**), and another **4,790** are passes with conditions.

points.h: Nearly every inspection ends in a pass

points.h: The last four years show the same summer peak

story.lead: Norway maple is Toronto's most common street tree.
story.summary: Toronto has **69,468** Norway maples on its streets. That is about one in every ten City-owned street trees, and about two and a half times the next tree, the honey locust. Maples of all kinds make up more than one in four street trees.
story.sub: Based on the City of Toronto street tree inventory: 688,335 City-owned trees on streets, current snapshot.

facts.label: Norway maples on Toronto streets
share of all street trees that are Norway maple
street trees in the maple group (genus Acer)

points.h: Norway maple leads, far ahead of any other tree
points.p: There are **69,468** Norway maples, against **27,758** honey locusts in second place. That is about **2.5 times** as many. Honey locust also shows up twice more in the list, as the Skyline and Shademaster types.

points.h: Maples as a group make up over a quarter of trees
points.p: Grouping trees by genus, a group of close relatives, puts maples (Acer) first with **185,621** trees. Honey locusts (Gleditsia) are next with **59,904**, and oaks (Quercus) follow with **51,575**. Maples have about three times as many trees as the second group.

points.h: Norway maples are found in every ward, most in Ward 2
points.p: Ward 2 has the most, **7,606** Norway maples. Ward 15 follows with **5,104**. Ward 13 has only **693**, so Ward 2 has about 11 times as many. Every one of the 25 wards has at least several hundred.

story.note: This counts only City-owned trees on streets, not trees in parks, ravines or private yards.

q: How fast does Toronto Fire arrive?

queries.purpose: Typical (median) response time by year, all calls

queries.sql: SELECT CAST(hour(alarm_time) AS VARCHAR) AS label, round(median(response_minutes), 1) AS value FROM fire_calls WHERE response_minutes IS NOT NULL AND response_minutes >= 0 GROUP BY hour(alarm_time) ORDER BY hour(alarm_time) LIMIT 30

story.lead: Toronto Fire typically arrives in about five minutes.
story.summary: The typical Toronto Fire response, from alarm to first truck arriving, is about **5 minutes**. That has barely moved since 2018, staying between **4.9 and 5.3 minutes**. Half of all calls get a truck faster than this, and half take longer.
story.sub: Based on every call Toronto Fire responded to, 2018 to 2024, using the middle (median) response time.

facts.label: Typical response time in 2024
Typical time for medical and fire calls
Typical time at 3, 4 and 5 a.m.

points.h: Response times have hardly changed since 2018
points.p: The typical time was **4.9 minutes** in 2018 and 2019. It peaked at **5.3 minutes** in 2022. In 2024 it was **5.1 minutes**, only about 12 seconds slower than in 2018.

points.h: Medical and fire calls get the quickest response
points.p: Medical and emergency fire calls both have a typical time of **5 minutes**. Hazardous materials and carbon monoxide calls take **6 minutes**. Non-emergency calls take longest, at **7.4 minutes**.

points.h: Trucks arrive a little slower overnight
points.p: From 8 a.m. to 9 p.m. the typical time is about **4.9 to 5 minutes**. Between 1 and 5 a.m. it rises to **5.7 to 5.8 minutes**. The gap is under a minute.

story.note: Response time is the time from the alarm to the first truck arriving. It is a middle value, so many calls take longer.

story.lead: New homes from permits peaked in 2021, then fell.
story.summary: Permits issued in 2021 created **15,109** new homes. By 2025 the figure was **2,063**, about one-seventh of the peak. Across 2017 to 2025, permits in this data created about **87,600** homes.
story.sub: Toronto building permits cleared (closed or finished) and issued 2017–2025, the full years.

facts.label: homes created by permits issued in 2021, the peak
homes created by permits issued in 2025

points.h: Homes created rose to 2021, then dropped sharply
points.p: From **9,163** homes in 2017, the number climbed to **15,109** in 2021. It then fell to **8,718** in 2022 and **4,180** in 2024. The 2025 figure of **2,063** is the lowest of the nine years.

points.h: Counting homes lost, the picture is the same
points.p: Some permits also remove homes. Taking those away gives **13,565** net new homes in 2021 and **1,363** in 2025. Over the nine years, about **10,950** homes were lost, so net new homes total about **76,700**.

points.h: Mixed-use and apartment buildings account for most new homes
points.p: Buildings mixing homes with shops or offices created **39,798** homes, and apartment buildings **28,518**. Together that is about **78%** of all homes created. Detached houses add **6,073**, and laneway or rear-yard suites **921**.

story.note: Only permits already closed or finished are in this data, so it may not cover every home permitted, especially in recent years.

story.lead: Broken bin lids are the top reason people call 311
story.summary: Damaged residential bin lids lead 311 requests: about **138,600** since 2019 once old and new names are added together. Garbage and waste services draw more than one in three of all requests (**36%**). Wildlife, property standards and potholes follow.

points.h: Waste services get more than one in three requests

points.h: In 2025, bin lids were still first, far ahead

story.lead: Coyote calls nearly doubled in two years.
story.summary: Animal Services logged **5,399** coyote requests in 2025, up from **2,781** in 2023. That is almost twice as many in two years. The 2026 count is only part of a year and already stands at **3,837**.

points.h: Animal Services coyote requests jumped in 2025

points.h: Coyote calls come in all months of the year

queries.sql: SELECT strftime(collision_time, '%A') AS label, count(DISTINCT collision_id) AS value FROM ksi_collisions WHERE collision_time IS NOT NULL GROUP BY strftime(collision_time, '%A'), isodow(collision_time) ORDER BY isodow(collision_time)

queries.purpose: Serious collisions by month of year (all years combined)
queries.sql: SELECT strftime(collision_time, '%b') AS label, count(DISTINCT collision_id) AS value FROM ksi_collisions WHERE collision_time IS NOT NULL GROUP BY strftime(collision_time, '%b'), month(collision_time) ORDER BY month(collision_time)

story.lead: Serious collisions peak in the evening rush hour
story.summary: Serious collisions are most common around 6 pm, with **531** in that hour over the years, against just **84** at 4 am. Nearly one in three (**31%**) happen between 3 pm and 8 pm. Fridays and the months from June to October are also busier.
story.sub: Collisions in Toronto where someone was killed or seriously hurt, 2006 to September 2026, all years combined.

points.h: The afternoon and evening are the most dangerous hours
points.p: Collisions climb through the day and peak at **531** in the 6 pm hour. That is about **six times** the **84** at 4 am, the quietest hour. The five hours from 3 pm to 8 pm hold **2,379** of the **7,620** collisions.

points.h: Friday is the worst day, Sunday the best
points.p: Friday has **1,216** serious collisions, the most of any day. Sunday has the fewest at **966**. Friday is about **26%** higher, but the weekdays are all fairly close to each other.

points.h: Summer and early autumn are the riskiest months
points.p: June is the highest month with **774** collisions, and February the lowest with **455**. June is about **1.7 times** February. June to October together account for **3,752** collisions, about half the total.

story.note: Each collision is counted once, however many people were involved. The months and weekdays add up all years together, and 2026 is only a partial year.
